passages.title: Sunday Mornings with a Camera
passages.passage:
Until last spring, I had never (1)____ much interest in photography. My uncle gave me his old camera when he bought a new one, and at first I left it in a drawer for weeks. Then one rainy Sunday, (2)____ there was nothing else to do, I took it out and walked around our neighbourhood. I was surprised by how (3)____ I enjoyed looking at ordinary things through the lens. A wet street, a cat on a wall, an old man selling bread – everything seemed more interesting than usual.

Since then, I (4)____ pictures almost every weekend. I have joined an online group (5)____ people share their photos and give each other advice. Some of the comments are quite honest, but I have learned to accept them (6)____ getting upset. My photos are still far from perfect. I often forget to check the light, and sometimes I press the button too early. However, I am (7)____ better than I was six months ago.

The hobby has changed my routine (8)____ well. I get up earlier, and I notice small details that I used to walk (9)____ without seeing. My mother says I am spending too much time on the camera and not enough on my homework. She may be right, but I think a hobby that makes you look (10)____ carefully at the world than before is worth a few hours a week.

questions.explanation: The collocation is take an interest in something. We do not say make, give or do an interest.
The clause gives the reason for taking the camera out, so a reason linker (as / because) is needed. So introduces a result, although a contrast and unless a condition.
How much I enjoyed measures the degree of a verb. Many goes with countable nouns, and very or too cannot follow how before a subject and verb.
Since then links a past starting point to now, which calls for the present perfect. A simple past or past continuous would cut the action off in the past.
The group is the place in which people share photos, so the relative adverb where fits. Which or whom would need to be the subject or object of the clause, and whose needs a possessed noun.
Without + -ing means the second action does not happen. Despite would wrongly suggest the writer does get upset, and unless or until make no sense here.
Get better is the everyday way to say improve. Go and turn are used for changes for the worse or for colours (go bad, turn red); make better needs an object.
The fixed phrase as well means also. Too and also already mean also on their own and do not combine with well.
You walk past something when you go by it without stopping. Over, through and across describe going on top of, inside or from one side to the other.
The sentence ends with than before, so a comparative is needed: more carefully. Most is a superlative, and much or very cannot be followed by than.

passages.title: The Night the Lanterns Went Up
passages.passage:
Every autumn, the village (1)____ my grandmother lives holds a lantern festival. It takes place on the first full moon after the rice harvest, and people from the nearby towns come to watch. This year I was allowed to help with the preparations for the first time.

The work started a week (2)____ the festival. Every family was (3)____ for making its own lanterns from bamboo and coloured paper, and the children were given the job of painting them. My cousin and I painted fish, birds and stars, (4)____ of them very neat, but nobody seemed to mind. Meanwhile, the men built a wooden stage in the square, and the women prepared enough food to feed the whole village.

On the evening itself, the square was so crowded (5)____ we could hardly move. There was a drum performance, a dance by the local school, and a long speech by the village head, (6)____ nobody listened to very carefully. At nine o'clock the lanterns were lit and carried down to the river. Hundreds of small lights floated away in the dark, and for a moment everyone (7)____ silent.

My grandmother told me later that the festival had almost been (8)____ up twenty years ago because so many young people had left the village. Fortunately, a group of teachers decided to keep it going, and now it is more popular (9)____ ever. I hope it continues, and I have already promised to come back next year, (10)____ busy I am.

questions.explanation: The relative clause tells us the place in which the grandmother lives, so where is needed. Which or that would need in before them, and whose shows possession.
A week before the festival gives a point of time measured back from an event. Ago counts back from now and cannot take an object; until and since describe a period, not a starting point.
The adjective that takes for and means having the duty to do something is responsible. Capable takes of, interested takes in, and proud takes of.
None of them is the pronoun used before of with a plural group. No must come directly before a noun, neither is for two things only, and nothing cannot take of them.
So + adjective + that expresses a result. As and than belong to comparisons, and which would start a relative clause with no noun to refer to.
The non-defining clause after the comma refers to the speech, a thing, so which is right. Who is for people, that cannot follow a comma in this kind of clause, and what does not refer back to a noun.
Fall silent is the collocation for suddenly stopping talking. Felt silent mixes up feel and fall, and made or held would need an object.
Give up means to stop doing something for good, which fits a festival that nearly ended. Take up means to start, put up means to build or raise, and call up means to telephone.
More popular than ever is a comparative, and comparatives are followed by than. Then is a common misspelling here, and as only pairs with as ... as.
However + adjective means no matter how, so however busy I am is correct. Whatever and whenever cannot be followed by an adjective, and although needs a full clause after it, not busy I am.

passages.title: Behind the Counter
passages.passage:
My grandfather (1)____ a small hardware shop on the corner of our street for more than forty years. It is not a large place – just one room with shelves that reach the ceiling – but he seems to know exactly (2)____ everything is. If a customer asks for a particular screw, he goes straight to the right box without looking.

When I was younger, I used to spend Saturday afternoons there. Grandfather (3)____ let me count the coins in the till, and if I did it correctly he gave me a sweet from the jar behind the counter. Later, he taught me how to (4)____ with customers: to greet them, to listen to what they needed, and never to make them feel foolish for asking a simple question.

These days the shop is much quieter. A big supermarket opened on the main road two years ago, and many people prefer to buy their tools there (5)____ it is cheaper. Grandfather does not complain, (6)____ I know he worries. He still opens at seven every morning and closes at six, (7)____ nobody has come in all afternoon.

Last month I suggested that he (8)____ sell some things online. He laughed and said he was too old for computers, but he did not say no. So now, every evening, I photograph a few items and put them on a website. We have (9)____ sold much yet, but last week a man from another city ordered three old brass door handles. Grandfather was so pleased that he told every customer (10)____ came in the next day.

questions.explanation: For more than forty years describes a period that continues up to now, so the present perfect has run is needed. Ran would mean the shop is closed, and the simple present or present continuous cannot take a for-period.
He knows the place of every item, so the indirect question needs where. When asks about time, whether asks a yes-or-no question, and which would need a noun after it.
Would + verb describes a repeated past habit, just like used to. Used needs to before the verb, and should or might do not describe habits.
The phrasal verb deal with people means to handle them. Treat takes a direct object with no with, and behave and manage do not combine with with in this meaning.
The clause gives the reason people choose the supermarket, so because fits. So introduces a result, although a contrast, and despite must be followed by a noun or -ing, not a clause.
Not complaining and secretly worrying are a contrast, so but joins them. So would make the worry a result of not complaining, and or or nor offer alternatives.
Even if means it makes no difference whether nobody has come, which fits keeping the shop open. Even so is an adverb, not a linker, as if compares, and in case gives a precaution.
After suggest that, the verb takes should or the bare form. Would and will do not follow suggest, and must would make it an order, not a suggestion.
Have not ... yet is the normal negative present perfect with yet. Never and hardly do not combine with yet, and no cannot stand between have and a past participle.
The relative pronoun is the subject of came and refers to people, so who is right. Whom is only an object, which is for things, and whose needs a following noun.

passages.title: The Deep End
passages.passage:
I did not learn to swim (1)____ I was fourteen, which is late in a town full of rivers. My friends had all learned as small children, and I was too embarrassed to admit that I could not. Whenever they went to the lake in summer, I made (2)____ excuse: a cold, a lot of homework, a visit to my aunt.

Everything changed when my school announced that swimming (3)____ be part of the sports programme the following year. There was no way to avoid it. That evening I told my father the truth, and instead (4)____ laughing, he offered to teach me himself.

Our first lesson was at the public pool early on a Saturday morning, when hardly anybody was there. I held (5)____ to the edge and refused to let go. My father did not push me. He simply stood in the water next to me and waited (6)____ I was ready. It took twenty minutes. After that, he showed me how to float on my back, and I was amazed to find that the water actually held me (7)____.

We went every weekend for two months. Some lessons went badly; once I swallowed so much water that I wanted to give (8)____ completely. But little by little I got (9)____ to the feeling of having nothing under my feet. By the end of the summer I could swim the length of the pool, slowly but without stopping.

When the school lessons began, I was not the best swimmer in the class, but I was no longer the boy who stayed on the bank. And I think my father was even (10)____ proud than I was.

questions.explanation: Not ... until (or till, before) marks the point at which the situation finally changed. When would say he did not learn at the age of fourteen, the opposite of the meaning.

Make an excuse is the collocation, and excuse is a countable noun that needs a determiner; some, another or every also work before the list of excuses. The fails because no particular excuse has been mentioned, and up fails because a bare noun cannot follow made up.

The announcement is reported after a past verb and refers to the following year, so will shifts back to would. Will breaks the sequence of tenses, and could or might are too uncertain for something there was no way to avoid.
Instead of + -ing is the only form: laughing did not happen and teaching did. Instead alone cannot be followed by an -ing form, and than or for do not follow instead.

Hold on to something means to grip it and not let go, which matches refused to let go; held tight / tightly / fast to are also accepted. Held out to or held up to mean offering or lifting, not gripping.
Wait until a clause happens is the pattern; till is the same word. For fails because wait for needs a noun or an object plus to-infinitive, not a subject and verb.
Hold somebody up means to support them so they do not sink, and afloat says the same thing. Down or back would mean the water pushed him under or stopped him, the opposite of floating.
Give up means to stop trying; give in, to admit defeat, also fits after a bad lesson. Give out means to distribute or run out, and give away means to hand something to someone.
Get used to + noun means to become familiar with something; accustomed is the formal equivalent. Use without -d is a common slip, and close or near would need a physical thing after to.

Than later in the sentence shows a comparative, and with proud the comparative is formed with more before the adjective (prouder is also possible, but only without the word proud following). Most is a superlative, and very or so cannot be followed by than.
